attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, given as part of his argument.

semantics.note: The paraphrase follows the words fairly well. But the sentence is a sweeping description of who holds power, used to argue that the situation 'cannot and should not stand.' It works as argument, not as a testable causal claim.

contract.note: The contract counts any contribution from outside experts as contradiction. Marcus's point is that the wider scientific community lacks insight, so only the two companies can act. Experts that OpenAI chose, gave access to, and whose findings OpenAI alone acted on fit his point rather than refute it. The contract's own ambiguity flags admit this, so its reading is stretched against him.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own report, March 15, 2023. It shows red teamers the company selected found risks that fed OpenAI's own safety work, and it withholds architecture and training details. That shows controlled participation, not insight for the scientific community or outside ability to act.

OpenAI launch announcement, March 14, 2023. It says expert feedback fed into OpenAI's mitigations. The companies still decided and carried out all fixes, so this does not refute the claim as Marcus meant it.
ARC's firsthand account, March 19, 2023, of dangerous-capability testing on access OpenAI granted. It is real outside work but depended on OpenAI and gave no independent ability to address the risks.

reviews.rationale: This is Marcus's endorsed, sweeping argument about how power is concentrated when models are kept secret, made to support a call for transparency. The contract scores it as refuted if any selected outside expert contributed. That reading is unfair, because work OpenAI chose to commission is consistent with the claim that only the companies can act. Read fairly, the statement is evaluative rhetoric with no measurable standard, so it is not scored. The evidence is context only.
